justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, starting near 92.1 for the one-day horizon and gradually rising to 93.0 at one month. This gentle upward slope likely reflects a baseline assumption of slight positive momentum or mean-reversion toward a perceived fair value slightly above current levels, combined with carry or drift effects typical of the asset class in question. The one-day estimate stays close to the last observed value because over very short horizons, prices tend to be anchored near their starting point, and any expected move is small relative to noise. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I allowed the point estimate to drift upward modestly, reflecting either a mild bullish tilt in the prevailing trend or fundamental factors suggesting gradual appreciation.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.7 units, reflecting typical intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the interval widens to about 8 units, and at one month it reaches roughly 18 units. These widths were calibrated to reflect historical realized volatility scaled by the square root of time, a standard approach under the assumption that returns are approximately independent across periods. I also incorporated some additional uncertainty beyond pure statistical volatility to account for model uncertainty and the possibility of regime changes.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macroeconomic shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a deterioration in credit conditions, or a geopolitical event — could drive prices well below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. Liquidity crunches or correlated selling across asset classes can produce moves far larger than historical volatility would suggest. On the upside, a positive surprise in economic data, a policy reversal, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above the upper bound. These tail events are by definition excluded from a 90% interval, meaning there remains a genuine 10% probability of outcomes outside the range, which in financial markets often corresponds to the most consequential scenarios worth monitoring closely.
